title: The Girl Who Carries the Market

pages.text: Ramatu arrived in the city market at dawn, as she did every day. She carried a large metal pan, the tool of a kayayo, a young woman or girl who carries shoppers’ loads on her head. A woman called, “Girl, carry my tomatoes!” Ramatu lifted the heavy basket and followed her through the noisy crowd, her neck steady and her feet quick.

pages.alt: A girl carries a heavy basket on her head through a crowded market at dawn.

pages.text: Ramatu had left her village in the north the year before, hoping to earn money for her family and for her own school things. In the city, she shared a wooden shed floor with other girls at night. Some days she earned enough for a meal, and some days she did not. She missed her mother’s cooking and her village school. “One day, I will go back to class,” she told herself.

pages.alt: A girl lies on a mat in a market shed at night with other girls sleeping nearby.

pages.text: Auntie Memunatu, a tomato seller, noticed the girl. “How old are you?” she asked kindly. “Thirteen,” said Ramatu. “Thirteen,” said Auntie. “Carrying loads is hard on a growing body.” She gave Ramatu a plate of rice and a place to sit in her stall in the shade. “Eat first,” she said. “Then we talk.” Ramatu ate slowly, and for the first time in weeks she felt cared for.

“Eat first,” she said.
“Then we talk.” Ramatu ate slowly, and for the first time in weeks she felt cared for.
pages.alt: A market woman offers a plate of rice to a girl beside a pile of tomatoes.

pages.text: On Saturdays, a volunteer teacher named Mr Kporha held a reading class under the market’s shade. Ramatu joined. She was behind, but she learned fast. She learned to read a price tag, then a sentence, then a short story. “You are clever,” said Mr Kporha. “Clever, and brave. Learning is your right, Ramatu.” Ramatu held her small exercise book to her chest like a treasure.

pages.text: Auntie Memunatu and Mr Kporha took Ramatu to see Madam Nkansah, a social welfare officer. Madam Nkansah listened, wrote carefully and explained. “In Ghana, every child has the right to education and protection,” she said. “Children should not be doing heavy work that harms them or keeps them from school. We will work with your family and find a safe place, and a school, for you.” Ramatu’s eyes filled with tears of relief.

We will work with your family and find a safe place, and a school, for you.” Ramatu’s eyes filled with tears of relief.
pages.alt: A social welfare officer speaks gently to a girl and two adults in a small office.

pages.text: Within weeks, Ramatu moved into a safe home for girls and began to attend school in the afternoons, with an evening class to catch up. She was in a class with younger children at first, and some of them giggled, but she did not mind. On Sundays, she visited Auntie Memunatu and carried nothing heavier than a bag of oranges. “I am learning,” she said. “I am learning very fast.”

pages.text: Ramatu wrote home with Mr Kporha’s help. “c/o Girls’ Home, Central Market Road, Accra. 12th May, 2027. Dear Mother, I hope you are well. I want to tell you some good news. I am now living in a safe home, and I am going to school every day. I miss you very much and I will come to see you during the holidays. Please greet everyone in the village for me. Your loving daughter, Ramatu.”

pages.alt: A girl writes a letter at a table with a teacher beside her and a small village photo.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: an informal letter still needs an address, even a temporary one such as “care of” a home. The date comes below it. Ramatu used full words and a clear order: news, feelings, a promise and greetings. Notice “Dear Mother” and “Your loving daughter”, a warm close for a parent. Every child has a story, and every story deserves to be written well. The end.
